learningObjective: Distinguish which decisions belong to compile-time (ahead-of-time lowering, kernel selection, memory planning) and which belong to run-time (dispatch, allocator calls, dynamic shape adaptation).
stem: Which statement best characterizes the boundary between the compiler and the runtime in a typical ML compilation stack (e.g., IREE, TVM, XLA)?

options.text: The compiler emits target-specific kernels and a lowered artifact whose scheduling, buffer plan and kernel selection are fixed; the runtime dispatches kernels, manages memory and streams, and services shape-dependent branches within the pre-planned strategy.
The compiler and runtime are the same component; both perform kernel selection, memory allocation and dispatch in a single execution phase where lowering happens each time an input tensor arrives.

The compiler owns memory allocation and stream scheduling at run time, while the runtime is a thin wrapper that only records timing events and forwards inputs to precompiled kernels without touching allocation or streams.

The compiler performs only front-end parsing (op resolution, type inference); every optimization pass — including fusion, tiling and kernel selection — is deferred to the runtime and re-executed on every invocation.

explanation: The canonical division of labor is: the compiler performs lowering, optimization, kernel selection and static memory planning ahead of time (or JIT-once), producing an artifact (bytecode, VM program, .so, plan file). The runtime consumes that artifact and handles device state at execution time — allocator calls, stream/event management, dispatch, and shape-dependent branches within the plan. Boundaries can shift (JIT vs AOT), but memory allocation and dispatch are runtime responsibilities in essentially every mainstream stack.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: describes the standard compiler-emits-artifact / runtime-executes-artifact split used by IREE, TVM, XLA, TensorRT, AOTInductor.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: conflates compiler and runtime; even JIT stacks separate the lowering phase from the execution phase.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: reverses the responsibilities. Compilers do not manage allocators or streams at run time.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: fusion, tiling and kernel selection are compile-time (or JIT-once) transformations, not per-invocation runtime work.

assumptions: A conventional two-phase (compile-then-run) ML system, not a purely interpreter-based one.
nonImplications: Does not imply that the boundary is rigid; some systems perform partial JIT specialization at first invocation, but the split of responsibilities still holds.
Does not imply that the runtime is stateless; runtimes typically own allocator pools, streams, and cached artifacts.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses AOT compile-time work with per-invocation dispatch.
